newsitem.title: ALBANIA: New Albania crisis looms over election.
newsitem.headline: New Albania crisis looms over election.

text.p: The chaotic Balkan state of Albania was teetering on the brink of fresh turmoil on Wednesday as President Sali Berisha said he would call elections and most political parties threatened to boycott them.
European envoy Franz Vranitzky, who brokered the latest political compromise at the end of last week, was set to arrive in Tirana on Thursday for yet more talks to save the elections.
Early elections have been planned since March and are aimed at preventing a slide back into the violence and rioting which erupted after the collapse of pyramid investment schemes.
The elections are a key part of the international effort to restore law and order in Albania. A multi-national military force is also in the country, protecting the supply of humanitarian aid.
Berisha said he would dissolve parliament and set June 29 as the election day, although a boycott by other parties would make a mockery of the vote.
"The day of June 29 will be one of the deepest victories of Albanian democracy," he told a crowd in the town of Kavaja, 50 km (30 miles) from Tirana and a stronghold of his support.
"We go to the elections sure that we will win and have one of the biggest victories for Albanian democracy," Berisha said.
Socialist Prime Minister Bashkim Fino, returning from a trip to Washington, said compromise was necessary.
"I think we have to overcome this crisis. We should talk with Vranitzky after his arrival today or tomorrow, with President Berisha and with the political parties," Fino told Albanian Television.
Albania, Europe's poorest country, has emerged only since 1990 from more than four decades of isolation and Stalinist rule.
As the political turbulence continued in Tirana, the Italian foreign ministry said it was calling an international conference on Albania on June 18.
It said the conference was likely to be at the level of foreign ministers and would be attended by more than 30 delegations including the United States.

The new crisis blew up after Berisha's Democratic Party, which has a big parliamentary majority, pushed through an election law which the other eight parties in the Government of National Reconciliation said favoured the former ruling party.

The other parties were unhappy over the division of seats between proportional representation and majority voting. They were also furious that the law was presented to parliament by the Democrats rather than by the national unity government.

The other parties in the government held a meeting and said they would stand by their threat to boycott the vote if it was held under the law pushed through by the Democrats. But they said the were still ready to work for a compromise.
"We will make attempts with political and institutional means (for compromise)," said Socialist Party chief Fatos Nano.
The Democratic Party insisted its law was in line with last week's Vranitzky deal and agreements with other parties.
The Socialists pulled out of the last elections in May 1996, which international observers said were flawed.

Another key point of the Vranitzky contract was the disbanding of so-called salvation committees, formed mostly in the south of the country at the time of the rioting to bring back order as the state administration collapsed.

The contract stipulated they should disband 46 days before the election, but they have said they will break up only if the elections are guaranteed to be free and fair. A meeting of the committees is due on Friday.
